articles.body: Even with more container vessels routing back through the Red Sea on Asia – Europe services, and estimations of slumping post-peak demand, carriers have been able to push rates up 10% to N. Europe and 23% to the Mediterranean over the past month. Prices ticked up 3% last week to $4,375/FEU to the Mediterranean and were about level at $3,595/FEU to N. Europe. Congestion in N. Europe hubs, as well as some lingering backlogs in the Far East may be helping put some degree of upward pressure on rates, with a recent one-day port worker union strike across many ports in Europe as well as other regions, possibly adding to backlogs. Carriers planned GRIs of $1,000 – $1,500/FEU for these lanes to start the month and additional increases for mid-November. Daily rates so far this week have stayed flat, but the coming days will indicate if carriers go through with the price hikes and if they’ll succeed, with some forwarders skeptical that market conditions will support further increases. Even with transpacific rates still at peak levels, carriers have GRIs of $2,000 – $3,000/FEU set to start the month for these lanes as well, though here too rates so far this week have not climbed and some forwarders think more increases are unlikely as this trade finally enters slow season. East Coast rates cooled 6% compared to last week’s bump, but are still $200/FEU higher than two weeks ago at about $9,900/FEU, with West Coast prices about level since climbing to the $8,300/FEU range in September. Asia – Europe rates are climbing relative to September, but from July to September prices fell $2,000 – $3,000/FEU on these lanes, about back to their pre-peak season baseline in mid-May. Meanwhile, the surprising rate resilience on the transpacific – including post-Golden Week, with prices currently about $5,500/FEU higher than before peak season – and the relatively short amount of time left until demand is likely to pick up ahead of Lunar New Year may make it unlikely that transpacific prices will fall back anywhere close to their pre-peak baseline before they climb again. Another factor that could help prop rates up even as demand cools is the potential port worker union strike at LA/Long Beach. The Local 26 watchmen union, part of the ILWU, has been working under an expired contract since mid-2025 and last week voted to authorize a strike as early as November 1st. Over the weekend though, the union agreed to extend the current contract until 5pm PT on November 4th to allow additional time for negotiations, with federal mediators now involved. A strike by the relatively small union could have an outsized impact on port operations as these workers provide required security services at many of the terminals. In air cargo, Far East – N. America rates continued to climb last week, increasing 9% to $7.76/kg from the peak season demand bump. This price level – a high for the year – is up 40% compared to this time last year, and is approaching the 2025 peak of $8.00/kg reached early last December. Asia – Europe rates were about level at $4.39/kg last week and are 11% higher year on year, but are well short of highs of about $5.25/kg seen earlier this year, as the market continues to adjust to decreases in e-commerce volumes on this lane. Judah Levine, Head of Research, Freightos Group (Nasdaq: CRGO)

articles.body: Europe Tankers Torm strikes eight-tanker newbuild deal in joint venture push Adis Ajdin November 4, 2026 0 0 1 minute read Torm Torm Danish product tanker giant Torm has stepped up its fleet expansion with agreements for eight LR2 newbuildings through a 50:50 joint venture. The Copenhagen- and New York-listed owner disclosed the latest contracts in its third-quarter results, confirming that the agreements were signed after the end of September. Torm has not identified its joint venture partner or the shipyard involved, while pricing and delivery dates for the eight vessels have also been left undisclosed. The move marks another major step in the company’s return to direct newbuilding contracts, following a series of investments in MR tankers at Chinese yards. Torm has also exercised options for two additional MR newbuildings during the third quarter, lifting its existing programme at China’s Zhoushan Changhong International Shipyard to eight firm vessels. The original six 50,000 dwt ships are scheduled for delivery in 2029, with the additional pair following in 2030. Shipbroking sources previously placed the scrubber-fitted vessels at around $46m apiece, valuing the full eight-ship programme at approximately $368m. Torm has since secured options for another two MR newbuildings, potentially extending that programme further. The latest investments build on a fleet renewal drive that has also seen the company acquire six MR resale newbuildings scheduled to join its fleet between 2027 and 2028. The owner has meanwhile continued to dispose of older tonnage, selling the 2007-built LR1 Torm Venture and the 2008-built MR Torm Laura during the third quarter. Those disposals left Torm with an operating fleet of 95 product tankers at the end of September, excluding vessels on order. articles.body: Asia Containers Shipyards Uncategorized Idan Ofer turns to Japan for boxship quartet Adis Ajdin November 4, 2026 0 104 1 minute read DryDel Shipping DryDel Shipping Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has been linked to an order for four midsize containerships at Japan’s Imabari Shipbuilding, marking a rare Japanese addition to its extensive newbuilding programme. Shipbuilding sources have identified the Singapore-based owner as the buyer of the quartet, which would take its containership orderbook to over 65 vessels worth more than $5.5bn. The move marks EPS’s first reported containership order in Japan in four years, with the company having concentrated much of its recent fleet expansion at Chinese yards. Details of the latest ships, including contract prices and delivery dates, have yet to emerge.EPS has emerged as one of the most active owners in the containership newbuilding market, building up a substantial orderbook across several vessel sizes. Last September, the company was linked to eight 6,000 teu vessels at Hengli Heavy Industry and China Merchants yards, with options for additional ships. The vessels were priced at close to $80m apiece, including scrubbers and high reefer capacity, with deliveries expected between 2027 and 2029. That followed another series of six 1,800 teu feeder ships at China Merchants Jinling Shipyard, reportedly costing around $30m each. The latest deal comes as Japan steps up efforts to rebuild its shipbuilding industry and regain ground lost to China and South Korea. Tokyo is targeting a doubling of annual shipbuilding capacity from around 9m gt to 18m gt by 2035, backed by a major government-supported investment drive. In September, Japan approved eight shipyard investment programmes representing around ¥900bn ($5.83bn) in planned public and private spending, including up to ¥311bn ($2bn) in government support. The funding is directed at dock expansion, automation, cranes and other production upgrades, with an Imabari-led group eligible for up to ¥113.8bn ($727m). Imabari has also strengthened its position through the acquisition of a 60% stake in Japan Marine United earlier this year, creating Japan’s largest shipbuilding group and the world’s fourth-largest by tonnage. The consolidation comes as Japanese yards face tight capacity, with industry figures showing almost no available construction slots through 2029. articles.title: Switch Maritime, Incat Crowther Secure US Agreement for Hydrogen Ferry
articles.summary: Switch Maritime and Incat Crowther have secured a Design Basis Agreement (DBA) with the United States Coast Guard (USCG) for their SWITCH-150 hydrogen fuel cell-electric fast ferry, marking a regulatory milestone in the development of the 150…
articles.body: Switch Maritime, Incat Crowther Secure US Agreement for Hydrogen Ferry Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 4, 2026 (Credit: Incat Crowther) Switch Maritime and Incat Crowther have secured a Design Basis Agreement (DBA) with the United States Coast Guard (USCG) for their SWITCH-150 hydrogen fuel cell-electric fast ferry, marking a regulatory milestone in the development of the 150-passenger vessel. The agreement establishes a regulatory framework to guide the vessel's construction, commissioning and eventual operation, with the design intended to deliver performance comparable to diesel-powered ferries while producing only water vapour as vessel emissions. The SWITCH-150 combines hydrogen fuel cell-electric propulsion with onboard hydrogen storage, allowing it to operate on high-frequency ferry routes without requiring shoreside charging infrastructure or changes to service schedules to accommodate charging. The vessel is designed to be refuelled using mobile hydrogen equipment, with a daily bunkering schedule. The 28.5-meter aluminium ferry will have a 9-metre beam and accommodation for 150 passengers and six crew members. Its propulsion system comprises six 225 kW fuel cells, four 588 kW electric motors driving four propellers and a 1,576 kWh battery system, supported by four compressed hydrogen tanks with a combined capacity of 720 kilograms. The vessel is designed for a service speed of 25 knots and a maximum speed of 27.5 knots. The hydrogen storage capacity is intended to provide sufficient range for a full day of operations across various New York ferry routes. The passenger deck will include seating for 150 people, luggage storage, a kiosk, three bathrooms, including a wheelchair-accessible facility, and large windows. The first SWITCH-150 is intended to operate in New York City, based at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, with the project supported by a $2 million grant from the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA). “Signing the DBA with the Coast Guard is a critical milestone in advancing the development of the SWITCH-150. With the DBA in hand, Switch, our project team, and the USCG have a clear and defined framework that will inform vessel construction, commissioning, and ultimately operation,” said Francisco Planells, Director of the Newbuild Program, Switch Maritime. The new design builds on the regulatory and operating framework established by Sea Change, the first hydrogen fuel cell-electric ferry in the United States, also designed by Incat Crowther. Sea Change received its USCG Design Basis Agreement in 2020 and its Certificate of Inspection in 2024, allowing it to begin passenger service in July of that year. For the SWITCH-150, the project team worked with the USCG to establish a framework demonstrating equivalent safety and risk mitigation measures for hydrogen propulsion and storage. The International Maritime Organization's Interim Guidelines for the Safety of Ships Using Hydrogen as Fuel, approved in May 2026, also provided a foundation for the agreement. With the DBA secured, Incat Crowther will move forward with detailed design development and preparation of a digital shipbuilding package for construction.

articles.title: Veth Propulsion Unveils New Thruster with Up to 7% Fuel Savings
articles.summary: Veth Propulsion by Twin Disc has introduced a new contra-rotating azimuth thruster designed for cruise vessels and ferries, with the company claiming fuel consumption reductions of up to 7% in real-world use.The new Streamline-CRP system is designed to improve hydrodynamic efficiency…
articles.body: Veth Propulsion Unveils New Thruster with Up to 7% Fuel Savings Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 4, 2026 Streamline CRP (Credit: Veth Propulsion) Veth Propulsion by Twin Disc has introduced a new contra-rotating azimuth thruster designed for cruise vessels and ferries, with the company claiming fuel consumption reductions of up to 7% in real-world use. The new Streamline-CRP system is designed to improve hydrodynamic efficiency, reduce emissions and minimize noise and vibration, including during operations in shallow-water conditions. The thruster incorporates a redesigned gearbox using combined push-pull technology to optimize water flow and reduce resistance, alongside a long, slender tail section intended to minimize drag. The system also features contra-rotating propellers designed to deliver balanced thrust and precise vessel control in all directions, while optimized propeller hub caps help reduce energy losses. Streamline-CRP is available in L-Drive, Z-Drive and compact integrated thruster configurations to accommodate different vessel designs. The system comes with a standard four- and five-blade propeller arrangement, with five- and six-blade or six- and seven-blade configurations available for specific applications. An integrated flange cover provides additional protection while reducing drag. “Customers across the marine industry are demanding solutions that deliver both performance and efficiency,” said Bastiaan van Zuijlekom, Managing Director of Veth Propulsion. According to the company, the combination of its propulsion technologies and hydrodynamic design improvements is intended to reduce operating costs and improve onboard comfort. Based in Papendrecht, the Netherlands, Veth Propulsion is part of Twin Disc and develops marine propulsion and maneuvering systems for inland, offshore and seagoing vessels.

articles.title: Preventing engine room fires before small defects become emergencies
articles.summary: BIMCO’s Tanker Safety Network recently examined how leaking pipes, inadequate insulation and electrical faults can develop into serious fires. Members shared practical experience and discussed the maintenance, technology and organisational support needed to reduce the risk. The network met online on 29 October 2026...
articles.body: Preventing engine room fires before small defects become emergencies in International Shipping News 04/11/2026 BIMCO’s Tanker Safety Network recently examined how leaking pipes, inadequate insulation and electrical faults can develop into serious fires. Members shared practical experience and discussed the maintenance, technology and organisational support needed to reduce the risk. The network met online on 29 October 2026 for a session on engine room fire prevention, combining three incident case studies with polling and an exchange of members’ experiences. The presentation highlighted the human, operational and financial consequences of engine room fires. Gard’s analysis of its hull and machinery fire and explosion claims for 2017–2024 found that nearly 60% originated in engine rooms. Learning from incidents Three cases illustrated how defects and weaknesses in protective measures can combine: • A failed fuel connection. A replacement pressure transmitter fitting with an unsuitable thread failed, allowing fuel to spray onto a turbocharger with missing insulation. The incident demonstrated the importance of both suitable replacement components and effective protection of hot surfaces • A hydraulic oil leak awaiting repair. A leak had been identified several hours before a fire, but repair was deferred until the vessel reached anchorage. The fire developed while the ship was still at sea, prompting discussion about assessing warning signs and deciding when action is needed • An electrical fault in a starter panel. Inspection following an auxiliary blower alarm revealed a burnt-out contactor and damage to associated electrical components. Worn contacts, loose connections and shortcomings in inspection and maintenance were discussed as possible contributing factors. The presentation also highlighted pipe supports, tightening procedures, filter covers and flexible hoses as areas requiring attention. Restoring insulation and protective arrangements after maintenance is an essential part of completing the job. Making prevention work in practice Members discussed the challenge of inspecting the large number of electrical components on board. Approaches shared included identifying critical equipment and incorporating inspection and servicing of contactors into the planned maintenance system. Participants also questioned how to capture risks elsewhere in the installation. Alongside these technical measures, participants raised wider questions about the availability of suitable spare parts, time to carry out repairs and support for less experienced engineers. They discussed how expectations about reaching the next port or anchorage might influence decisions to delay maintenance. Earlier detection and reliable response Thermal imaging was discussed as a way to identify hot surfaces and gaps in insulation that may be missed during visual inspections. Members also considered the potential of AI-assisted cameras and other monitoring technology to provide earlier warnings. The discussion underlined the need to connect detection with action. In one of the cases presented, the leak was already known before the fire occurred. Earlier warnings therefore need to be accompanied by an appropriate response, supported by effective watchkeeping, maintenance and decision making. Members also raised a question about the continued availability of local water mist firefighting systems if a fire disrupts the main electrical supply. The role of an emergency power supply was discussed, with the issue remaining open for further examination. Continuing the discussion Members shared additional experience of fires involving incinerators, tumble dryers and electrical equipment in accommodation spaces. Power banks and lithium-ion battery fires were suggested as a possible topic for a future session. The Tanker Safety Network provides a forum for members to exchange operational experience and discuss common safety challenges. Members are encouraged to propose topics and share lessons from their operations. Source: BIMCO, https://www.bimco.org/news-insights/bimco-news/2026/10/29-engine-fires/ 2026-11-04 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Guangzhou targets routine methanol bunkering, regional coordination in International Shipping News 04/11/2026 Guangzhou is seeking to turn green methanol bunkering demonstrations into a routine service by streamlining operating procedures, connecting fuel suppliers with buyers, and improving regulatory coordination with Shenzhen and Hong Kong, a port authority official told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. The southern Chinese port completed green methanol deliveries to a bulk carrier, a container ship, and a car carrier within 40 days in September and October, providing experience to expand the service, Wu Jia, a staff member of Guangzhou Port Authority, said in an interview. “We hope to move beyond pilots and demonstrations toward routine bunkering in the future,” Wu said. The authority’s priorities include reviewing the three operations to make subsequent deliveries more efficient and facilitating discussions among marine fuel suppliers and users. “We need to sum up experience from these three bunkering operations and streamline the procedures to improve operational efficiency,” she said. “We want to provide a platform for dialogue among the parties involved in marine energy and help bring suppliers and buyers together.” Wu also called for closer coordination among Guangzhou, Shenzhen, and Hong Kong, noting that the Daqing 268 bunker vessel had already delivered in all three locations. “We hope to advance the alignment of regulatory practices and rules across the three places in the Greater Bay Area, to enable seamless and convenient green fuel bunkering across the region,” she said. The interview did not specify a timetable for routine methanol service or contracted supply volumes. Platts assessed Low-carbon methanol FOB Shanghai at $815/mt on Oct. 29, unchanged day over day. Broader bunkering coverage Guangzhou’s first green methanol bunkering operation took place Sept. 6, when Daqing 268 supplied 1,021 mt to the bulk carrier Green Future at Dayushan anchorage, according to the port authority. The fuel carried is ISCC EU-certified. On Sept. 28, the same bunker ship supplied 300 mt of green methanol to the container ship COSCO Shipping Carnation at Nansha’s phase II terminal, establishing a berthside service alongside the anchorage option. The operation allowed container handling outside the restricted bunkering area to proceed during refueling, avoiding a separate trip to an anchorage, Nansha maritime authorities said in a Sept. 30 statement. The port added a third vessel category Oct. 16, when the car carrier Guang Rong received 1,400 mt of bonded green methanol at Nansha’s automotive port, according to Guangzhou Port Authority. The authority said the operation made Guangzhou the world’s first port to have carried out green methanol bunkering for container ships, bulk carriers, and car carriers. Demand guides fuel infrastructure Guangzhou’s infrastructure planning is being shaped by shipping companies’ fuel requirements and the different needs of ocean-going and regional vessels, Wu said. “Only by grasping fuel demand can ports develop targeted planning and layout for alternative fuels,” she said. “We believe each port has its own geographic advantages and resource endowments, which shape its choice of alternative fuel supply pathways.” Guangzhou can already supply LNG, biofuel bunkers, and green methanol, Wu said, with a range of fuel infrastructure needed to serve different vessels. “We think it is crucial for ports to build infrastructure for a range of green fuels, because visiting vessels have diverse needs,” she said. The port is also working with Los Angeles to develop a transpacific green shipping corridor. The ports signed a cooperation MOU in October 2023 covering the corridor, digital supply-chain infrastructure, and other emissions-reduction initiatives. Los Angeles reiterated Guangzhou’s status as a green corridor partner in a July 9 announcement. For regional shipping, Guangzhou is prioritizing vessel electrification and the facilities needed to support it. “Within the Greater Bay Area, our focus is on planning and building charging and battery-swapping facilities for vessels,” Wu said. According to the port authority, Guangzhou Port has also rolled out electrification across all links of its operations: the battery-electric tug Suigang Diantuo 01 entered service in April 2025, and full shore-power berth coverage was achieved in December 2025. A battery-powered container shipping route linking Nansha and Hong Kong International Terminals commenced operations on Oct. 13. The inaugural sailing was operated by Sui Gang Dian Hang 02, part of a series of ships equipped with containerized batteries and charging and battery-swapping capabilities. Source: Platts 2026-11-04 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: “We hope to move beyond pilots and demonstrations toward routine bunkering in the future,” Wu said.
The authority’s priorities include reviewing the three operations to make subsequent deliveries more efficient and facilitating discussions among marine fuel suppliers and users.
“We need to sum up experience from these three bunkering operations and streamline the procedures to improve operational efficiency,” she said.

articles.title: GPS Jamming in Contested Waters Demands an All-Source Operational Maritime Picture
articles.summary: GPS Jamming Has Become Routine in Contested Waters Operations in degraded environments are no longer a planning scenario. For anyone responsible for a maritime operational picture, they are already the operating condition in much of the water European navies patrol. GPS jamming touched 124,235 distinct vessels...
articles.body: GPS Jamming in Contested Waters Demands an All-Source Operational Maritime Picture in International Shipping News 04/11/2026 GPS Jamming Has Become Routine in Contested Waters Operations in degraded environments are no longer a planning scenario. For anyone responsible for a maritime operational picture, they are already the operating condition in much of the water European navies patrol. GPS jamming touched 124,235 distinct vessels worldwide in Q3 2026, up 11.7% on the previous quarter, according to Windward’s Q3 2026 maritime risk report. September was the busiest month of the year, and the Black Sea alone accounted for 30% of the jamming Windward observes worldwide. GPS Jamming Is an Area Problem, and It Changes What Every Vessel Reports GPS jamming is an area-level event. Interference degrades satellite navigation signals across a zone, and every receiver inside it is affected, whatever the ship and whoever owns it. Because a vessel’s AIS position comes from its own satellite navigation receiver, every ship in that zone can end up broadcasting a position that is wrong. In August 2026, Windward found that 393 of the 642 transits logged through the Strait of Hormuz, 61.2%, never happened. Jamming corrupted AIS positions and produced transits that no ship made. Windward’s Q2 2026 risk report counted 3.35 million false ship-to-ship meetings generated by GPS jamming worldwide since late February 2026. One case from May shows how this looks in the data. Two tankers off Fujairah appeared to meet. Both vessels’ AIS positions had jumped onto the same two spoofed coordinates. At the same instant, one of them was reportedly meeting hundreds of other ships at the same point. No meeting had happened. Read as vessel behavior, it would have been a false lead. Read as an area event, it was filtered out. That distinction matters for a navy. A watch officer who reads jamming as vessel behavior chases ghosts and suspects ships that did nothing wrong. One who ignores jamming altogether lets real activity hide inside the noise. AIS Spoofing Is a Vessel Choice and Behavior Exposes It AIS spoofing is a different problem. It does not happen to a ship because of where it sails. It is a choice made on a specific vessel to broadcast a false position or a false identity. A case from September shows the difference. The Philippine Coast Guard accused a Chinese-flagged research vessel of spoofing its location while it held station about 38 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat in Batanes, over cable corridors in the Luzon Strait. According to the coast guard, the vessel’s AIS showed it moving from the coast of Xiamen to a location off Papua New Guinea on the same day, and its behavior was consistent with marine scientific research rather than transit. Windward data showed the vessel’s AIS destination field reading “TOWING 1NM CABLE”. The Chinese Embassy in Manila said the ship was conducting normal operations in waters under Chinese jurisdiction. No area effect explains a reported track like that. The broadcast and the vessel’s physical presence disagreed, and the disagreement belonged to one ship. Identity spoofing works the same way. The IMO’s list of falsely flagged ships reached 613 at the end of Q3 2026, and the list includes 27 fraudulent registries. A false flag is broadcast by choice. Behavior is what exposes it. A reported track that jumps an impossible distance, a position no other sensor confirms, a destination field that reads like survey gear, or a flag no registry recognizes all point at the vessel rather than the area. Separating that from jamming is the first analytical step, and it decides whether a ship is treated as a suspect or a bystander. All-Source Operational Intelligence Holds the Picture When One Source Fails No single source survives a degraded environment on its own. AIS fails under jamming and misleads under spoofing. Satellite imagery has revisit gaps and weather limits. RF detection confirms that an emitter is present but not always who it belongs to. What holds is the combination. All-source operational intelligence fuses AIS with whatever sources the mission requires. That can mean SAR and EO satellite imagery, RF detection, dark vessel detection, registry and ownership data, years of behavioral history, or any other source that sharpens the picture. When one input degrades, the others check it. Windward’s Q2 2026 risk report made the same point for conflict zones — positional data should be treated as adversary-influenced until independently verified, and telling a deliberate evader from a ship caught in interference means correlating the gap with imagery, ownership, and voyage behavior. The result is a picture an operator can trust because it does not depend on any one feed being honest. Integration Matters More Than Another Dashboard Navies do not need another screen. They need the picture inside the systems they already run, from national C2 to the mission and combat management systems that shipbuilders and integrators deliver. That makes integration the real test in procurement. A capability that demands rip-and-replace, or adds a separate dashboard that watch officers have to check alongside everything else, rarely survives contact with an operational workflow. Windward’s intelligence is built to be consumed outside its own interface. Its API is GraphQL-based, so integrators can request exactly the fields a mission system needs. Webhooks push events such as risk score changes and alerts on vessels of interest into existing systems as they happen. Risk indicators are traceable to the evidence behind them, so an assessment stays auditable once it leaves the platform, and the API is designed to sit alongside a customer’s own data rather than replace it. For navy program and acquisition managers, that means the capability can arrive through the mission and combat management systems their shipbuilders and integrators already deliver, rather than as a new system to procure, accredit and support. For the shipbuilders and system integrators themselves, it means adding fused maritime intelligence to what they offer a navy without building or maintaining it in-house. Deployment models and data residency requirements differ by country and programme, and they are worth raising early in any conversation. Bring Your Degraded-Environment Questions to Hall 6 GPS jamming is not a scenario to plan for. It is the condition navies already operate in, and AIS spoofing rides on top of it. The answer is a maritime picture built from all-source intelligence that holds when one source fails and arrives inside the systems navies already run. Windward is at EURONAVAL through November 6 in Hall 6, booth J128. Book a meeting to see how the picture holds up in contested waters. Source: Windward 2026-11-04 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: MarineSolar sets sights on wider commercial deployment of NanoDeck® solar technology
articles.summary: MarineSolar Energy Solutions is moving into wider commercial deployment of its NanoDeck® solar technology while continuing development of its next generations, and has appointed Mijs Verhoeven as Director of Strategic Relationships to strengthen engagement with shipowners, ship managers and operators internationally....
articles.body: MarineSolar sets sights on wider commercial deployment of NanoDeck® solar technology in International Shipping News 04/11/2026 MarineSolar Energy Solutions is moving into wider commercial deployment of its NanoDeck® solar technology while continuing development of its next generations, and has appointed Mijs Verhoeven as Director of Strategic Relationships to strengthen engagement with shipowners, ship managers and operators internationally. Solar power is well established on land, but adoption aboard commercial vessels has remained limited. Ships present a demanding operating environment and conventional solar solutions were not originally designed around the practical realities of operating at sea. MarineSolar has approached the challenge from the shipping side. Rather than adapting a conventional land-based solar panel, NanoDeck® has been engineered specifically around the operational and environmental requirements of commercial vessels. From development to commercial deployment NanoDeck® has progressed through extensive development, independent testing and trials at sea, including a pilot installation aboard Rio Tinto’s 204,950 dwt Newcastlemax RTM Cook. The current generation is commercially available today, with the next generation becoming available from January 2027. Current technology achieves solar conversion efficiency of up to 23%, while MarineSolar’s longer-term development roadmap targets approximately 32% within the next three to five years. Further generations are already in development to improve performance and extend the technology across a wider range of surfaces, operating environments and vessel segments. NanoDeck® installations can be upgraded or replaced as newer generations become available, allowing owners to benefit from future developments in the technology. Depending on vessel type, configuration, available surface area, trading routes and operating profile, MarineSolar says onboard solar can contribute to a reduction of up to 5% in a vessel’s overall emissions. Chris Russell, Chief Technical Officer, said: “NanoDeck® technology allows for both traditional solar energy gathering via a battery and a unique direct power system for greater efficiency without the need for a battery all housed to withstand the rigors of the marine environment. Following the success of the technology NanoDeck® is moving to increase energy efficiency and energy density to provide a 20% uplift in delivered power per m2 in the next 6 months. A hugely exciting time to be to be taking our unique product forward to the marine markets.” Solar alongside shipping’s future fuels Shipowners are making investment decisions today about vessels that may still be operating ten or fifteen years from now. Yet which alternative fuels will dominate, how widely they will be available, what they will cost and how regulation will develop remain difficult to predict. Solar does not depend on a single future fuel pathway. Whatever fuel a vessel ultimately uses, electricity generated onboard can reduce the amount of energy that needs to come from that fuel. Solar can also operate alongside batteries, wind-assisted propulsion and other efficiency technologies. MarineSolar therefore sees solar not as an alternative to shipping’s emerging energy solutions, but as a technology that can complement them. Marc Roberts, CEO, said: “Most commercial vessels have surfaces that could be generating electricity, yet today very few of them are. We see real commercial potential right across the fleet, from retrofits on existing ships to newbuilds where solar can be designed in from the start. Because solar works alongside whatever fuel, battery or wind-assisted technology an owner chooses, it lets them start reducing fuel costs and emissions now, without having to bet on a single future pathway.” Building the business case The potential for solar differs for every vessel and operation. Available surface area, energy demand, trading routes, solar irradiation and time spent sailing and in port all influence how much electricity can realistically be generated. MarineSolar uses this data to assess both retrofit and newbuild projects, calculating expected solar generation and its potential impact on fuel consumption, emissions and operating costs. The result is a tailor-made solution of how solar could contribute to the individual vessel or operation, both technically and commercially. Joep Groot, COO, said: “Owners want a business case based on their own operations, not on generic assumptions. With the MarineSolar Atlas we calculate what NanoDeck™ will generate on the routes their vessels actually trade and what that means for their fuel consumption and return on investment. After installation, our cloud monitoring shows the actual performance, so the business case is measured rather than assumed.” As commercial deployment develops, MarineSolar is preparing its production, installation capabilities and supply chain to support future projects. Ian Pilkington, Chief Supply Chain Officer, said: “As we prepare MarineSolar to scale commercial installations, we are strengthening our electrical systems engineering capability so that ongoing advances in PV module and power conversion technology feed directly into our future products. That means higher performance and more choice for our customers, both offshore on vessels and onshore across shipyard sites. We are also building a global, end-to-end supply chain to ensure consistent supply and raise the level of service we offer the maritime industry.” Strengthening commercial engagement As part of that commercial push, MarineSolar has appointed maritime professional Mijs Verhoeven as Director of Strategic Relationships. Verhoeven will work with owners and managers to identify where solar could contribute across individual vessels and fleets, understand their longer-term energy strategies and connect potential projects with the appropriate technical expertise within MarineSolar. She has worked in the international maritime industry in both in-house and independent roles spanning business development, marketing and PR. Through her company Helmswoman, she has built an extensive international network across the maritime industry. Mijs Verhoeven, Director of Strategic Relationships, said: “What excites me is how much potential there already is today, and how much further we can take it. NanoDeck® gives us something tangible to bring to the market now, while the ongoing development will continue to broaden where and how solar can be applied across shipping. At a time when the industry is still navigating the energy transition and the future fuel mix remains uncertain, I think that makes solar particularly interesting. The ambition to develop MarineSolar into a broader solar energy provider for shipping makes this an incredibly exciting time to join the company.” Source: MarineSolar 2026-11-04 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Ships present a demanding operating environment and conventional solar solutions were not originally designed around the practical realities of operating at sea.
MarineSolar has approached the challenge from the shipping side.

Green shipping is among the visit’s focus areas, with the Danish delegation visiting both APM Terminals Mumbai and the Mazagon Dock shipyard. Danish-operated ships made more than 3,000 calls at Indian ports in 2025. This illustrates how important India is as a market for Danish shipping. Its importance will only increase as the Indian economy grows. Danish shipping is seeing growth in India across several segments, including container, dry bulk and tanker shipping. “India is becoming an increasingly important partner for Denmark – economically, te­ch­no­lo­gi­cal­ly and geopolitically. The country has major ambitions in areas including green shipping, renewable energy and artificial intelligence. Denmark has strong expertise that can contribute to India’s transition. I am travelling to India to learn from the pace and scale of its development, strengthen our partnerships and open doors for Danish businesses,” says Minister for Business, Com­pe­ti­ti­ve­ness and Maritime Affairs Martin Lidegaard (Our translation, Ed.) in a press release. Danish Shipping welcomes the visit. “It is wise for the minister responsible for maritime affairs and the Danish Government to focus on strengthening cooperation with India. The visits to APM Terminals and Mazagon Dock highlight Danish companies’ involvement and provide an opportunity to strengthen cooperation with Indian authorities and businesses. Closer ties between Denmark and India can create new opportunities for shipping. Favourable conditions for investment, access to competitive shipyards, cooperation on greener ports and ships, and responsible ship recycling are all areas where closer cooperation can create significant value in both countries,” says Anne H. Steffensen, CEO of Danish Shipping. ‘’ Closer cooperation can create significant value in both countries’’ Anne H. articles.body: Construction has started on the completion of the docks at the Port of Taureana di Palmi, a EUR 7.5 million project awarded to SILEM, Società Italiana Lavori Edili Marittimi, with a duration of 20 months. The works will finish the shoreline docks and enclose the entire perimeter of the port waterway, expanding available space on land and at sea, increasing the number of berths and improving navigation, safety and the quality of services. Starting the works required a complex administrative and operational process to clear the affected waterways and land areas, involving six concessionaires who had to vacate them. The Port System Authority will seek alternative solutions and spaces so that nautical activities can continue wherever possible during construction, limiting disruption to operators. The land areas will be redeveloped and reorganised, with yards paved in porphyry slabs and the services needed to run the new infrastructure. Garages for nautical activities and facilities for boaters will be built, with space for restaurants, yacht clubs, commercial activities and restrooms. The aim is for the port to become a welcoming hub linking port, city and sea, supporting tourism and the enhancement of the Costa Viola. The project has been made possible by close cooperation with the Municipality of Palmi. Environmental and landscape measures are a defining part of the design. Material from excavation and dredging will be reused to nourish a stretch of coastline north of the port, reducing disposal needs while helping protect the shoreline. New green areas will be created behind the caissons, using native species to form dune systems that serve both environmental and landscape purposes. President Paolo Piacenza said the start of works confirms the Port System Authority’s commitment to delivering on its promises to redevelop the whole port system, and that the project began within the timeframe the Authority set itself after careful planning and complex preparatory work. He added that the goal goes beyond completing a port project: it is to build infrastructure that interacts with its surroundings and becomes a hub for recreational boating and a new attraction for the entire Costa Viola.

articles.title: Palm Oil Cargo Operations: Getting the Cargo Details Right
articles.summary: Palm oil and its derivatives may not be classified as hazardous cargoes but carrying them successfully is not always straightforward. Preserving cargo quality requires good preparation, careful temperature management and close monitoring from the moment the tanks are prepared until discharge is completed. Palm oil is...
articles.body: Palm Oil Cargo Operations: Getting the Cargo Details Right in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 04/11/2026 Palm oil and its derivatives may not be classified as hazardous cargoes but carrying them successfully is not always straightforward. Preserving cargo quality requires good preparation, careful temperature management and close monitoring from the moment the tanks are prepared until discharge is completed. Palm oil is particularly sensitive to water, contamination, oxidation and changes in temperature. If the cargo is allowed to cool too much, it may begin to solidify and become difficult to pump. If temperatures fluctuate around its melting point, the cargo can separate into heavier and lighter layers. This may result in inconsistent samples, solids collecting near the bottom of the tank and problems during stripping or discharge. Excessive or uneven heating can be just as damaging. Localised hot spots around the heating coils may cause discolouration or deterioration, while heating the cargo too quickly can create significant temperature differences within the tank. The aim is therefore not simply to keep the cargo warm, but to heat it gradually and evenly, following the agreed heating instructions and the requirements of the particular grade being carried. Water is another major concern. It may enter the cargo through tanks or pipelines that have not been properly dried, condensation inside the tank, seawater ingress or leaking heating coils. Even a relatively small amount of moisture can affect cargo quality and contribute to an increase in free fatty acids. Tanks, lines and pumps should therefore be clean, dry and carefully inspected before loading, while heating coils should be pressure-tested and any cleaning chemicals fully removed from the cargo system. The vessel’s previous cargoes and the condition of the cargo system also need careful consideration. Tanks should be suitable for carrying edible oils, coatings should be in good condition, and incompatible materials should not come into contact with the cargo. Different grades must also remain properly segregated, with particular attention paid to common pipelines, stripping arrangements and sampling points. articles.body: KPMG secures mandate to lead Kuwait Ports Authority’s new strategic plan in Port News 04/11/2026 KPMG in Kuwait has been appointed to lead the development of Kuwait Ports Authority’s (KPA) Strategic Plan under Tender No. 3/2025/2026. articles.body: Africa Containers Cameroon’s Gulfcam taps new chief to drive Camship expansion Adis Ajdin November 4, 2026 0 105 1 minute read Gulfcam Gulfcam Cameroon’s Gulfcam is pursuing plans to acquire six vessels to expand its coastal container shipping operations between Kribi and Douala, with a former Camship executive taking charge of the business. Bernard André Ndengue took over as chief executive on November 1, replacing Albert Roger Boum, who stepped down last month to head Puma Energy’s operations in the Republic of Congo. Ndengue, a veteran of the country’s maritime sector who previously held senior positions at Cameroon Shipping Lines (Camship), has been tasked with developing Gulfcam’s container shipping arm and pushing ahead with its coastal shipping ambitions. The Douala-based group outlined plans in March to acquire six vessels to increase capacity between Cameroon’s two main ports, with the aim of capturing around half of the container freight currently transported by road along the corridor. The planned expansion would cover both domestic coastal trade and transshipment cargo, allowing containers discharged from larger vessels at the deepwater port of Kribi to reach Douala by sea rather than by truck.No investment figure, vessel specifications or acquisition timetable has been disclosed. Gulfcam announced the relaunch of its Camship service earlier this year, bringing in the chartered containership Atlantic Runner II to support operations between the two ports. The company’s initial operating plan envisaged a 10-day round voyage, at least three monthly calls and a target of 2,000 teu per round trip, including laden and empty containers. Actual sailing frequencies and cargo volumes have yet to be confirmed. The service has its roots in a weekly link launched by Camship-CLGG in November 2020, which operated until 2022. Gulfcam itself was established in 2021 through the merger of Camship-CLGG and petroleum transport and distribution business Gulfin. Camship traces its history to the former state-owned Cameroon Shipping Lines, which was privatised in 1997 before combining with local logistics group CLGG in 2008. The renewed coastal shipping push comes amid further investment in container logistics at Kribi. articles.title: Greenland’s scrubber ban sparks calls for wider Arctic crackdown
articles.summary: Greenland is moving to ban scrubber wastewater discharges throughout its territorial waters, prompting environmental groups to call for similar restrictions across the Arctic and ultimately a global prohibition. The country’s parliament, Inatsisartut, voted unanimously last month to direct the government to introduce...
articles.body: Environment Europe Regulatory Greenland’s scrubber ban sparks calls for wider Arctic crackdown Sam Chambers November 4, 2026 0 161 1 minute read Greenland is moving to ban scrubber wastewater discharges throughout its territorial waters, prompting environmental groups to call for similar restrictions across the Arctic and ultimately a global prohibition. The country’s parliament, Inatsisartut, voted unanimously last month to direct the government to introduce a phased ban covering ports, internal waters and territorial seas extending 12 nautical miles offshore. Discharges from open-loop scrubbers will be prohibited from July 1, 2027, followed by closed-loop and hybrid systems from July 1, 2029. The restrictions will require affected ships to switch to compliant fuels or retain scrubber wastewater onboard while operating in Greenlandic waters. “The decision by Greenland’s parliament to ban scrubber discharges is an important step towards cleaner shipping, and a clear signal for other countries to do the same,” said Kaare Press-Kristensen, senior advisor at Green Global Future. Sian Prior, lead advisor to the Clean Arctic Alliance, is urging the IMO to introduce a global ban, starting with the environmentally sensitive Arctic. The alliance also wants Iceland, Norway and Canada to adopt similar restrictions. Greenland’s decision follows Denmark’s prohibition on open-loop discharges in July 2025, with Sweden and Finland introducing similar measures. The move also goes beyond the 2025 OSPAR agreement, which mandates phased restrictions in ports and internal waters but currently only recommends extending them to territorial seas. Environmental campaigners are additionally backing a proposed green shipping corridor between Nuuk and Reykjavík requiring vessels to burn marine gas oil. articles.body: Europe Operations MPC Oceanic strikes deal for 41% of Marlow Navigation Adis Ajdin November 4, 2026 0 218 1 minute read Marlow Navigation Marlow Navigation Hamburg-listed MPC Oceanic Group has agreed to acquire a 41% stake in Cyprus-based shipmanager Marlow Navigation in a deal that will also see Marlow’s existing shareholders take a holding in the German maritime investment and services group. The transaction, announced on Wednesday, builds on a relationship spanning more than a decade between the two companies and will give Marlow’s current shareholders an approximately 9% stake in MPC Oceanic through the issuance of new shares. Marlow’s existing owners will retain majority control, with the Limassol-headquartered company continuing to operate independently under its established brand and leadership. Financial terms of the acquisition have not been disclosed. The deal brings MPC Oceanic closer to one of the world’s largest crew management providers, with more than 16,000 seafarers serving onboard vessels at any given time and crewing services covering over 1,150 ships worldwide. Marlow also employs more than 1,300 shore-based staff across 13 countries. For Marlow, the investment forms part of a generational transition at the company founded by Hermann Eden, who remains chairman, while opening up access to MPC Oceanic’s investment capacity, technology and wider maritime services network. MPC Oceanic chief executive Constantin Baack said the partnership would strengthen the group’s position in crew management and training, particularly as more complex propulsion systems, alternative fuels and tightening regulations place greater demands on seafarers. The move adds another major shipmanagement business to MPC Oceanic’s portfolio, which already includes Wilhelmsen Ahrenkiel Ship Management. In December 2023, the group, then operating as MPC Capital, joined forces with Wilhelmsen Ship Management to acquire Hamburg-based Zeaborn Ship Management, which had around 100 vessels under management at the time. MPC adopted its current name in September this year, reflecting its expansion beyond investment management into ship operations, maritime services and energy infrastructure. The group currently manages and operates more than 400 vessels and energy assets. For Marlow, the deal marks a fresh ownership development four years after it abandoned plans to merge with fellow Cyprus-based Columbia Shipmanagement. The two companies had explored a combination since 2017 but called off the proposed merger in October 2022, having continued to operate independently throughout. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: TotalEnergies As global pressure mounts to curb greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, France’s energy giant TotalEnergies has revealed a trio of new partnerships across geographies, joining forces with national oil companies (NOCs) in Malaysia, Angola, and India to share its cutting-edge methane-tracking technology and drive toward a near-zero emissions future by 2030. During the meeting of the Oil and Gas Decarbonization Charter (OGDC) member companies in Abu Dhabi, TotalEnergies has highlighted its cooperation with national oil and gas companies to reduce methane emissions through its partnerships with Petronas in Malaysia, Sonangol in Angola, and Oil India Limited (OIL) in India. To this end, the French firm has signed a collaboration agreement with Petronas, the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC) , and JGC Corporation to contribute to the development of the Southeast Asia Methane Emissions Technology Evaluation Center (SEA METEC), which will be a regional center based in Malaysia and dedicated to evaluating methane emissions measurement and monitoring technologies across Southeast Asia. The two companies are working together to identify concrete solutions to reduce methane emissions and flaring, improve energy efficiency, support facility electrification, and advance carbon management solutions. The cooperation is also covering greenhouse gas emissions reporting, technical training, and knowledge sharing, as well as the exploration of financing opportunities, including potential support from the World Bank’s Global Flaring and Methane Reduction (GFMR) Fund. A second month-long campaign will extend the use of AUSEA to additional OIL-operated sites, further strengthening the cooperation between the two companies on methane emissions reduction. articles.body: Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha (K Line) reported a sharp increase in profit for the first half of fiscal year 2026, supported by improved earnings from Ocean Network Express (ONE). Operating revenue reached JPY602 billion during the six months ending 30 September 2026. This was up 20.3% from JPY500.5 billion in the same period last year. Ordinary income from the segment climbed to JPY74.4 billion from JPY22.1 billion. K Line said short-term freight rates increased as the Middle East situation and port congestion tightened the balance between vessel supply and demand. The second quarter accounted for JPY68.9 billion of the segment’s first-half ordinary income. K Line’s containership fleet remained unchanged at 36 vessels as of 30 September. The fleet comprised 12 owned and 24 chartered ships, including twelve vessels of 14,000 TEU and eleven of 8,000 TEU. K Line also expects full-year containership ordinary income of JPY107 billion, compared with its previous forecast of JPY53 billion. The company expects the container shipping market to remain uncertain during the second half. However, short-term freight rates are projected to remain above the levels assumed in its previous forecast. K Line’s outlook does not assume a full return to Suez Canal transits during FY2026, although ONE plans to resume passage on selected services. The company expects conditions around the Strait of Hormuz to normalise towards the end of March 2027.

articles.title: Coal shipments to India drop 7%
articles.summary: "Between January and October, coal shipments to India dropped 7% y/y due to the increased cost of imports. Thermal coal demand has remained strong, particularly from the power sector, but domestic mining has not kept pace, forcing power plants to draw down inventories.
articles.body: Coal shipments to India drop 7% Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 4, 2026 Chart courtesy BIMCO "Between January and October, coal shipments to India dropped 7% y/y due to the increased cost of imports. Thermal coal demand has remained strong, particularly from the power sector, but domestic mining has not kept pace, forcing power plants to draw down inventories. In contrast, coking coal demand growth has eased following a decline in steel production amid low margins,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO. The cost of imported coal has increased due to a weaker rupee and higher coal prices. Prices have firmed due to increased demand following disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. As LNG supplies have tightened, the EU, Japan and South Korea have boosted electricity generation from coal. Furthermore, Chinese imports increased at the end of the second quarter following a mining accident that led to mine closures for inspections and thus lower production. Indian coal demand has firmed this year, driven by an approximate 9% y/y increase in coal-fired electricity generation. While electricity generation from solar and wind has also increased, the impact on coal demand has been minimal as hydroelectric generation has fallen due to a weaker monsoon linked to El Niño conditions. While, domestic coal production has increased by only around 4% y/y, inventories, rather than imports, have compensated and supported demand growth. By 1 November, 48% of Indian coal-fired power plants had critically low coal inventories. “As the world’s second-largest coal importer, accounting for 17% of global coal shipments, India’s weaker import demand has weighed on the wider market. However, the impact has been particularly pronounced for the supramax segment, whose coal shipments to India have fallen 16% y/y. Panamaxes have fared better, with volumes falling only 4% y/y, as they increasingly competed with other ship segments for coal cargoes,” says Gouveia. However, after several months of weaker shipments, Indian coal import demand appears to have firmed, with shipments rising 7% y/y in October. Critically low inventories have likely increased pressure on power plants to secure sufficient coal supplies, while power shortages may have further encouraged purchasing. In the coming months, high electricity demand, paired with the need to rebuild inventories, could support India’s coal import demand. “Looking ahead, the International Energy Agency expects Indian coal demand to only grow by 2.5% in 2027. Although the country is expected to see rising electricity demand and industrial activity, a recovery in hydroelectric generation could limit gains. Indian coal imports are also expected to increase only slightly, as growing domestic coal mining may limit import demand,” says Gouveia.

articles.body: Luxury Cruise Dream Unravels as Ship Forces Passengers Ashore Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 4, 2026 Villa Vie Odyssey (Credit: Villa Vie Residences) After disembarking more than 200 passengers who had paid tens of thousands of dollars to live on board for years, the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship departed Cambodia early on Wednesday. Last week, the vessel's owner, Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, suspended operations and forced passengers off the ship at the port town of Sihanoukville, saying ‌fuel price increases from the Iran war had made operations prohibitively expensive. The ship left with no passengers and around 50 crew, according to Taing Sochitkrishna, head of the Sihanoukville tourism department. He said around 100 passengers remained in Cambodia, while the others largely flew to other destinations in the region. Passengers unloaded their last belongings from the vessel on Tuesday, and many said they did not expect to return to the ship. "There are still many things on the ship that I wish I could take with me," said Shirine Thomas, of Wilmington, North Carolina, shortly after collecting some final items. The Villa Vie Odyssey had been cruising the world for at least 755 days as one of only a handful of ships that offered passengers the opportunity to rent or buy long-term or even permanent residences on board. The ship's final destination was unconfirmed. Some passengers and maritime tracking websites indicated the ship was bound for Singapore. Villa Vie Residences did not respond to emails or phone calls seeking comment. Sixty-seven-year-old retired high school teacher Mary Ann Demsar from Ontario, Canada, said the owners had provided no information on whether the voyage would continue. "We don't get any clear indication from the owners of Villa Vie as to what is happening," she said. "They've been so quiet, the only information we get is from the wonderful government and the representatives here in Cambodia." (Reuters - Writing by Josh Smith; Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan)

articles.body: Vessels & Vehicles November 4, 2026 · 1 minute ago Sea1's first methanol-ready offshore energy support vessel fitted with offshore crane and helideck NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Sea1 Diamond. Source: Sea1 Offshore Sea1 Offshore's first of four 120-meter-long offshore energy support vessels (OESVs) being built in China has been fitted with an offshore crane and helicopter deck, with delivery expected in January. Norwegian offshore services provider Sea1 Offshore placed the order for the first two OESVs with Cosco Shipping in November 2024, revealing at the time that negotiations were ongoing for the delivery of more vessels. The contract for the construction of two additional vessels was announced in March 2025. The construction of the first vessel, named Sea1 Diamond, began in September 2025, with the second, named Sea1 Citrine, following in December . Sea1 Diamond, launched at the yard in July , is currently undergoing outfitting and commissioning at the COSCO Nantong Shipyard, with the offshore crane and helicopter deck installed, as Sea1 Offshore reported on November 3. According to the Norwegian firm, the 250 T Huisman crane is designed for subsea lifting operations down to 3,000 meters, while the helicopter deck is dimensioned for Sikorsky S-92. The vessel is expected to be delivered in January 2027. Sea1 Offshore also reported that the OESV is still uncommitted and open for clients after delivery. Based on the ST-245 design, the OESVs will have a cargo deck of 1,400 square meters, and each will be equipped with a 250-ton deck crane, two remotely operated vehicle (ROV) hangars, and a moonpool. articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd targets 1.7 million TEU in Africa by 2030
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd aims to increase its annual container transport volume in Africa to 1.7 million TEU by 2030, as the German shipping company continues to expand its operations across the continent. The carrier announced that its African transport volumes surpassed 1 million TEU for the first time in 2026. The milestone...
articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd aims to increase its annual container transport volume in Africa to 1.7 million TEU by 2030, as the German shipping company continues to expand its operations across the continent. The carrier announced that its African transport volumes surpassed 1 million TEU for the first time in 2026. The milestone reflects the company’s growing presence in a market it considers central to its long-term expansion strategy. Hapag-Lloyd currently serves 27 African countries. Meanwhile, the company is marking 20 years of operations in South Africa, one of its most established markets on the continent. South Africa supports wider African expansion Hapag-Lloyd opened its first dedicated office in South Africa in 2006. Since then, it has expanded its local operations and customer network. Today, the company employs 52 people in the country. The acquisition of Deutsche Afrika-Linien’s container liner business in 2022 strengthened its connections between South Africa, Europe and the Indian Ocean. Rogelio Busto, Managing Director South & East Africa at Hapag-Lloyd, said the company’s development in South Africa has been supported by long-standing customer relationships and its local workforce. The carrier has also expanded its presence in other African markets. In 2021, it acquired NileDutch, strengthening its position in West Africa. Furthermore, Hapag-Lloyd established a dedicated Sub-Region Africa in 2024 to support business development and improve coordination across the continent. Hapag-Lloyd strengthens port partnerships More recently, Hapag-Lloyd expanded its cooperation with DP World to secure long-term terminal capacity in Dakar, Luanda and Dar es Salaam. The cooperation also supports infrastructure development in Banana and Maputo. These arrangements form part of the carrier’s efforts to strengthen its African transport network. Jesper Kanstrup, Managing Director Sub-Region Africa at Hapag-Lloyd, described Africa as an important growth market for the company. According to Kanstrup, Hapag-Lloyd plans to expand its network and capacity in line with customer demand while maintaining service quality and reliability. The carrier’s target of 1.7 million TEU by 2030 represents a significant increase from the transport volume milestone reached in 2026. However, Hapag-Lloyd has not disclosed an exact figure for its 2026 African volumes beyond confirming that they exceeded 1 million TEU.

articles.title: Cadeler's Wind Apex WTIV Set for First Assignment at Dogger Bank C
articles.summary: Cadeler has signed a firm contract to support turbine transportation and installation at the 1.2 GW Dogger Bank C offshore wind project in the UK, with its newbuild Wind Apex wind turbine installation vessel (WTIV) scheduled to join the campaign…
articles.body: Cadeler's Wind Apex WTIV Set for First Assignment at Dogger Bank C Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 4, 2026 (Credit: Cadeler) Cadeler has signed a firm contract to support turbine transportation and installation at the 1.2 GW Dogger Bank C offshore wind project in the UK, with its newbuild Wind Apex wind turbine installation vessel (WTIV) scheduled to join the campaign in the third quarter of 2027. The contract will mark the first deployment of Wind Apex following its delivery from the shipyard, according to Cadeler. The vessel will work alongside the project's existing installation vessel, providing additional capacity for the transportation and installation of Dogger Bank C's 87 offshore wind turbines. Wind Apex will also be available for deployment across the remaining phases of the wider Dogger Bank development. Wind Apex is the third vessel in Cadeler's A-class series, following Wind Ally and Wind Ace. The vessels are designed to support both foundation and turbine installation campaigns, combining high deck load with high crane capacity. "The campaign will also mark the first deployment of Wind Apex, and we look forward to seeing her begin operations on a project of this scale," said Mikkel Gleerup, CEO of Cadeler. Dogger Bank C is the third 1.2 GW phase of the 3.6 GW Dogger Bank Wind Farm, located approximately 130 kilometers off the north-east coast of England. The project is a joint venture between SSE (40%), Equinor (40%) and Vårgrønn (20%). SSE is leading development and construction on behalf of the partners, while Equinor will operate the wind farm following completion, with an expected operational life of around 35 years. Once all three phases are completed, Dogger Bank is expected to generate enough renewable electricity to power approximately six million UK homes annually. Cadeler has previously worked with SSE on the Beatrice and Seagreen offshore wind farms in the UK and will also work on the Equinor-partnered Bałtyk 2 and Bałtyk 3 offshore wind projects in Poland.

articles.title: ONE lifts full-year profit outlook after strong second quarter
articles.summary: Ocean Network Express (ONE) reported a net profit of US$1.32 billion for the second quarter of FY2026, up from US$285 million in the same period last year. Revenue increased to US$6.27 billion from US$4.46 billion, supported by higher cargo volumes and stronger freight rates. EBITDA more than doubled to US$1.99...
articles.body: Ocean Network Express (ONE) reported a net profit of US$1.32 billion for the second quarter of FY2026, up from US$285 million in the same period last year. Revenue increased to US$6.27 billion from US$4.46 billion, supported by higher cargo volumes and stronger freight rates. EBITDA more than doubled to US$1.99 billion, while operating profit rose to US$1.36 billion. The Singapore-headquartered carrier transported 3.4 million TEUs during the quarter, compared with 3.26 million TEUs a year earlier. Its average freight rate increased to US$1,709 per TEU from US$1,252. Higher ship, variable and bunker costs partly offset the improvement. ONE’s average bunker price reached US$749 per tonne during the quarter, up from US$518 a year earlier. First-half profit reaches US$1.35 billion For the first half of FY2026, ONE generated revenue of US$10.81 billion, compared with US$8.5 billion during the same period last year. Net profit reached US$1.35 billion, up from US$371 million. First-half EBITDA increased to US$2.69 billion, while operating profit rose to US$1.43 billion. ONE said strong Transpacific demand was supported by US inventory restocking and imports of data-centre equipment and industrial materials. Demand also remained firm across Latin American and intra-Asian trades. On the Asia-Europe trade, volumes remained stable. However, increased capacity and the gradual return of vessels to the Suez Canal placed pressure on the supply-demand balance and caused freight rates to soften. “Q2 delivered a strong financial performance, contributing to a solid first half of FY2026,” said Till Ole Barrelet, CEO of Ocean Network Express. “These results reflect our teams’ success in growing cargo volumes and achieving higher utilisation despite a challenging operating environment,” he added. ONE raises FY2026 outlook ONE raised its full-year net profit forecast to US$2 billion, more than double its previous estimate of US$900 million. The carrier now expects FY2026 revenue of US$21 billion, compared with its previous forecast of US$19.4 billion. Its EBITDA forecast increased from US$3.6 billion to US$4.7 billion, while the operating profit outlook doubled to US$2.2 billion. ONE expects spot freight rates to ease during the second half as cargo demand weakens seasonally. However, the carrier anticipates that rates will remain above the levels assumed in its previous forecast, with a modest increase expected ahead of the Chinese New Year. The outlook assumes that current operating conditions in the Strait of Hormuz will continue until the end of FY2026 and that Suez Canal transits will gradually resume. ONE operated 280 vessels with a combined capacity of 2.27 million TEUs at the end of September. The carrier’s orderbook comprised 51 vessels, including long-term chartered newbuildings.

articles.title: Piraeus container throughput returns to growth in third quarter
articles.summary: Container throughput at Pier I of the Port of Piraeus returned to growth during the third quarter of 2026, despite remaining significantly lower across the first nine months of the year. Piraeus Port Authority (PPA) said third-quarter throughput at Pier I increased by 0.3%, or 524 TEUs, compared with the same period...
articles.body: Container throughput at Pier I of the Port of Piraeus returned to growth during the third quarter of 2026, despite remaining significantly lower across the first nine months of the year. Piraeus Port Authority (PPA) said third-quarter throughput at Pier I increased by 0.3%, or 524 TEUs, compared with the same period in 2025. This marked the terminal’s first positive quarterly performance of 2026. Volumes improved more strongly during August and September, rising by 11.5%, or 10,161 TEUs. PPA attributed the recovery partly to new container-handling agreements with Piraeus Container Terminal and Pier I’s main customer. The agreements took retroactive effect from July and include revised tariffs and handling volumes. During October, Pier I handled five additional containerships and 7,843 TEUs under the agreement with Piraeus Container Terminal. Nine-month container volumes remain lower Despite the third-quarter recovery, Pier I handled 394,338 TEUs during the first nine months of 2026. This represented a 27.8% decline from 546,399 TEUs in the corresponding period of 2025. Local container volumes fell by 34.1% to 131,799 TEUs. Revenue from Pier I decreased by 26% to €34.8 million, while the segment recorded a pre-tax loss of €3.9 million. In the same period last year, Pier I generated a pre-tax profit of €6.5 million. However, revenue from the concession of Piers II and III increased by 3.2% to €70.7 million. During the third quarter alone, concession revenue rose by 9% compared with the same quarter of 2025. PPA revenue and profit decline PPA’s total revenue decreased by 8.2% to €178.8 million during the first nine months. EBITDA fell by 16.9% to €92.6 million, while profit after tax declined by 21.5% to €59.7 million. In the third quarter, revenue reached €66.9 million, down 7% year on year. Net profit fell by 17% to €24.3 million. PPA invested €126.6 million during the nine-month period, an increase of 84.5% compared with the previous year. The port authority said geopolitical developments in the Middle East affected container demand and trade flows, particularly during the first half of 2026. PPA added that the return of containerships to the Suez Canal was becoming more established during the fourth quarter. The company expects canal transits to increase over the coming months and estimates that traffic could fully recover by May 2027.

articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard has detained the cruise ship MSC Poesia at PortMiami, forcing MSC Cruises to cancel an 11-night Caribbean voyage after the vessel remained in port for two...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Pjotr Mahhonin/CC BY-SA 3.0 The U.S. Coast Guard has detained the cruise ship MSC Poesia at PortMiami, forcing MSC Cruises to cancel an 11-night Caribbean voyage after the vessel remained in port for two days. The Panama-flagged cruise ship was detained Sunday, November 1, during what the Coast Guard described as an expanded examination of the vessel. The ship had been scheduled to depart Miami that afternoon but remained docked with passengers aboard as inspectors reviewed its compliance with maritime regulations. In a statement released Tuesday, the Coast Guard said Sector Miami personnel were verifying the vessel’s compliance with international standards and U.S. regulations. “The Coast Guard is tasked with verifying safe and secure commerce,” the agency said, adding that the Captain of the Port’s priority is protecting passengers, crew, the vessel and the environment. The Coast Guard has not disclosed what prompted the expanded examination or identified any specific deficiencies. It also has not indicated when the ship might be cleared to depart. MSC Cruises confirmed Tuesday that it was canceling the voyage after efforts to resolve the issue proved unsuccessful. “Prior to departure, a regulatory matter arose that required resolution,” MSC Cruises said in a statement reported by NBC News. The company said it was unable to resolve the matter in time for the sailing to proceed. The cruise line said affected passengers would receive full refunds and assistance arranging their journeys home. Guests have also been permitted to remain aboard until noon Thursday, November 5, while making alternative travel arrangements. The canceled itinerary was scheduled to visit Jamaica, Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica, Honduras and Belize before returning to Miami on November 12. The detention raises questions about the nature of the regulatory issue that prevented the ship from sailing. Under the Coast Guard’s port state control program, foreign-flagged vessels calling at U.S. ports are subject to examinations to verify compliance with applicable international conventions and U.S. requirements. Serious deficiencies can result in a vessel being detained until the necessary corrective actions are completed. However, neither the Coast Guard nor MSC Cruises has publicly explained what inspectors discovered aboard MSC Poesia , leaving the reason for the detention unclear. Built in 2008, the 92,627-gross-ton MSC Poesia is part of MSC Cruises’ Musica class. The 294-meter vessel has capacity for 3,223 passengers and approximately 1,039 crew members. The ship underwent a major refurbishment earlier this year, including the addition of MSC’s Yacht Club luxury accommodations and upgrades to its dining and wellness facilities. There has been no indication that the refurbishment is connected to the detention. The ship’s next scheduled voyage is a 10-night Caribbean cruise departing Miami on November 12. MSC Cruises has not announced any changes to that sailing. As of Tuesday, the vessel remained in Miami, with no publicly announced timetable for its release.
