articles.title: Top 8 Freight Brokerage Services of 2026: Compared by Fit
articles.summary: The short answer C.H. Robinson is the largest freight brokerage in North America, with $11.56 billion in 2025 gross brokerage revenue, followed by Total Quality Logistics (TQL) at $7.36 billion and J.B. Hunt at $7.08 billion, according to the Transport Topics 2026 Top Freight Brokerage Firms list. This guide compares...
articles.body: The short answer C.H. Robinson is the largest freight brokerage in North America, with $11.56 billion in 2025 gross brokerage revenue, followed by Total Quality Logistics (TQL) at $7.36 billion and J.B. Hunt at $7.08 billion, according to the Transport Topics 2026 Top Freight Brokerage Firms list . This guide compares seven of the largest brokers on that list plus one managed freight specialist for mid-market shippers, ordered by shipper need rather than size. Two 2026 events change how shippers should read any broker list. On May 14, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that brokers can face state negligence claims for hiring unsafe carriers. On October 5, C.H. Robinson agreed to buy RXO in a deal valued at about $5.8 billion, expected to close in the first half of 2027. A freight broker arranges transportation using carriers it hires; it does not haul the freight itself. Every broker must hold FMCSA broker authority and keep $75,000 in financial security on file. Editor’s top 3 picks C.H. Robinson: best for multimodal scale. The No. 1 broker by revenue says it works with 450,000 contract carriers and manages 37 million shipments a year. Best for: large shippers that want one partner across modes and borders. Total Quality Logistics: best for high-touch truckload service. Its gross brokerage revenue rose 8% in 2025, the fastest growth in the top three, and its stated mission is service 24/7/365. Best for: recurring truckload lanes. WWEX Group: best for small and mid-sized shippers. The parent of Worldwide Express, GlobalTranz and Unishippers is the only top-10 broker whose Transport Topics listing includes parcel. Best for: shippers mixing parcel, LTL and truckload. How the largest brokers compare Revenue and rank come from the Transport Topics 2026 list, which ranks North American brokers by 2025 gross brokerage revenue. TT rank Broker 2025 gross brokerage revenue Operating model Best for 1 C.H. Robinson $11.56B Non-asset, global Large multimodal shippers 2 Total Quality Logistics $7.36B Non-asset, private Recurring truckload lanes 3 J.B. Hunt (ICS) $7.08B Brokerage arm of an asset-based carrier Brokerage plus intermodal 4 WWEX Group $5.18B Multi-brand 3PL with a UPS relationship SMB parcel and LTL 5 RXO $4.23B Asset-light, tech-led Enterprise truckload and last mile 6 Echo Global Logistics $4.00B Tech-enabled 3PL, private Self-serve plus full service 8 Landstar System $2.62B Agent network plus owner-operators A local agent relationship Reviews: 8 freight brokerage providers 1. TLI What it is: An Exton, Pennsylvania, managed transportation provider that has served manufacturers and distributors for more than 30 years. Best for: Shippers moving LTL and/or truckload freight regularly who want a dedicated account team. TLI runs LTL, truckload, expedited and multimodal programs, with freight claims management and invoice audit included, backed by 30,000-plus vetted carriers. In 2025 it recovered $1.2 million through freight claims and $634,608 through freight bill audits. Its latest transportation RFP results came in 18.2% better than generic carrier blanket rates, and its proprietary diesel table keeps fuel surcharges from becoming a carrier profit center. Strengths: a 4.9-star rating across 440-plus Google reviews; shippers stay 10.5 years on average. Watch-outs: pricing runs as all-in rates or a management fee, so confirm which structure fits your program. Standout: named the “World’s Greatest 3PL” in a 2026 “World’s Greatest” segment on Bloomberg TV. 2. C.H. Robinson What it is: A non-asset logistics provider founded in 1905 in Eden Prairie, Minnesota. Best for: Large shippers wanting truckload, LTL, intermodal and global forwarding under one contract. It ranks No. 1 with $11.56 billion, down slightly from $11.73 billion in 2024, and reports 75,000 customers and 37 million shipments a year. Its RXO purchase is expected to close in the first half of 2027. Strengths: the widest carrier network here; Navisphere platform. Watch-outs: RXO integration ahead. Standout: scale across modes and borders. 3. Total Quality Logistics What it is: A private, non-asset brokerage founded in 1997 by Ken Oaks in Cincinnati. Best for: Recurring truckload lanes needing an account team around the clock. TQL moved from No. 3 to No. 2, growing gross brokerage revenue from $6.82 billion to $7.36 billion. The company reports 9,000-plus employees across 60-plus offices in 26 states. Strengths: strongest growth in the top three; dry van to bulk coverage. Watch-outs: limited public financials; no owned trucks. Standout: 24/7/365 service as a core promise. 4. J.B. Hunt (Integrated Capacity Solutions) What it is: The brokerage segment of J.B. Hunt, headquartered in Lowell, Arkansas. Best for: Shippers pairing brokered truckload with owned intermodal capacity. It ranks No. 3 with $7.08 billion, nearly flat year over year. Brokerage is one of five segments alongside Intermodal, Dedicated, Final Mile and Truckload, and in 2023 J.B. Hunt agreed to buy BNSF Logistics’ brokerage operations. Strengths: owned intermodal capacity; J.B. Hunt 360 platform. Watch-outs: no air or expedited on its Transport Topics listing. Standout: brokerage and rail intermodal in one company. 5. WWEX Group What it is: A Dallas-based 3PL behind Worldwide Express, GlobalTranz, Unishippers, JEAR Logistics and BLX Logistics. Best for: Small and mid-sized shippers moving parcel, LTL and truckload together. It ranks No. 4 with $5.18 billion and reports 130,000-plus customers, more than 70 million shipments a year and a strategic relationship with UPS. Strengths: parcel on its Transport Topics listing; strong LTL focus. Watch-outs: no rail or intermodal listed; confirm which brand holds your contract. Standout: parcel and freight in one relationship. 6. Echo Global Logistics What it is: A Chicago-based, technology-enabled 3PL founded in 2005 and owned by The Jordan Company since 2021. Best for: Self-serve quoting for routine loads plus support for complex ones. It ranks No. 6 with $4.00 billion. On March 25, 2026, it completed its acquisition of ITS Logistics; the two had about $5.2 billion in combined 2025 revenue. Strengths: EchoShip self-service platform; new drop-trailer and drayage capabilities. Watch-outs: ITS integration is recent. Standout: self-serve and managed brokerage in one provider. 7. RXO What it is: An asset-light transportation company in Charlotte, North Carolina, spun off from XPO in 2022. Best for: Enterprise shippers wanting truck brokerage, managed transportation and last mile. It ranks No. 5 with $4.23 billion and bought Coyote Logistics from UPS for $1.025 billion in 2024. Its 2025 revenue of about $5.7 billion included $4.2 billion from truck brokerage. Strengths: RXO Connect platform; last-mile reach. Watch-outs: pending sale to C.H. Robinson, with no stated changes to contracts or rates. Standout: brokerage and last mile under one roof. 8. Landstar System What it is: A Jacksonville, Florida, transportation company built on independent commission sales agents. Best for: Shippers wanting a local agent backed by a national network. It ranks No. 8 with $2.62 billion. Agents find freight and coordinate moves, while capacity comes from owner-operators leased exclusively to Landstar and from other trucking companies and railroads. Strengths: distinctive agent model; flatbed, reefer, air and intermodal coverage. Watch-outs: service depends on your agent. Standout: local relationships at national scale. How to choose the right freight broker Authority and bond: Search the broker’s MC number on FMCSA’s SAFER system and confirm a $75,000 BMC-84 bond or BMC-85 trust is on file. Carrier vetting: Since the Montgomery ruling, ask what the broker checks before tendering a load, such as safety ratings and insurance. Mode fit: Match your freight mix to each broker’s listed freight types; not every large broker covers parcel, intermodal or air. Backup capacity: Ask whether the broker can fall back on owned trucks or containers in a tight market. Deal activity: Ask whether a pending merger affects your contract, rates or contact, and get the answer in writing. Our verdict C.H. Robinson is the safest default for large shippers that need every mode and global reach. For recurring truckload lanes where responsiveness matters most, TQL is the strongest alternative, while small shippers mixing parcel and LTL will get the most fit from WWEX Group. If you want owned backup capacity, shortlist J.B. Hunt; if you value one local contact, look at Landstar. Whichever you choose, verify FMCSA authority and ask how the broker vets carriers. Frequently asked questions What is the largest freight broker in the U.S.? C.H. Robinson, with $11.56 billion in 2025 gross brokerage revenue on the Transport Topics 2026 list, and it has extended its Lean AI agents to ocean and air freight . TQL is second at $7.36 billion, and J.B. Hunt is third at $7.08 billion. Can a freight broker be sued if its carrier causes a crash? Yes. In Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II , decided May 14, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 9-0 that federal law does not block state negligence claims against brokers for hiring unsafe carriers. The ruling does not make brokers automatically liable. What is the difference between freight brokerage and managed transportation? Freight brokerage arranges shipments load by load. Managed transportation is an ongoing program in which a provider handles carrier sourcing, execution, freight audit, claims and reporting for the shipper.

November 3, 2026 © Moxie Media Moxie Media will host its first dedicated user event, Moxie Connect: User Conference 2026, a complimentary event open to all maritime professionals, on Wednesday, December 2, at the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center in New Orleans, alongside the International WorkBoat Show. Moxie Connect will allow customers and maritime organizations to see the platform in action, with demonstrations on user experience, mobile and offline learning capabilities, maritime training content and tools for managing workforce training. The event will also explore the growing connection between training and competency management. Trainingportal includes capabilities that can help organizations establish role-based requirements, manage assessments and maintain evidence of competency alongside training records. The program will also introduce Mentor AI, Mintra’s AI solution, and discuss practical applications for using AI and digital learning tools to support continuous learning and workforce readiness. Moxie Connect will also feature an Integration Partner Showcase, demonstrating how Trainingportal connects with vessel management systems to share training and competency information across an organization’s systems. A regulatory update session will provide an industry perspective on current developments affecting maritime organizations. Additional sessions will address the future of Moxie’s maritime training content, including new and upcoming Coast Guard-related courses and other resources supporting maritime training and compliance. The event is open to existing Moxie customers as well as maritime organizations interested in learning more about Moxie, Mintra and Trainingportal. As an added benefit, registered attendees will receive a complimentary International WorkBoat Show exhibit hall pass, allowing participants to attend the morning event and then visit the WorkBoat exhibition. articles.title: Longer Navy Deployments Demand More Than Tough Sailors
articles.summary: By Chris Servello (OpEd) Ten and eleven month Navy deployments may become the norm for the next couple of years. That’s the message Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle and Master Chief...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman talk with U.S. Sailors during an all-hands call at Naval Air Station Sigonella, Sicily, Italy, Oct. 5, 2026. (U.S. Navy photo by Joey Rolfe) By Chris Servello (OpEd) Ten and eleven month Navy deployments may become the norm for the next couple of years. That’s the message Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy (MCPON) John Perryman delivered this past week. It’s not particularly good news, but it’s news that Sailors and their families deserve to hear. Credit to both leaders for being upfront about it. For years, the Navy has struggled to meet growing operational demands with too few ships . Deployments get extended , maintenance schedules slip and crews spend more time away from home than anyone originally planned. None of this is new, but hearing the Navy’s senior leadership acknowledge that longer deployments may be the standard rather than the exception is important. As MCPON Perryman pointed out, uncertainty is often what makes these deployments especially hard. A family can prepare for ten months apart. It’s much harder to prepare for seven months that becomes eight, then nine, then ten, with each extension arriving just as homecoming seems within reach. Admiral Caudle is also right that the lasting solution is a bigger Navy with more capacity and flexibility. We’ve needed that for years, and the urgency has only grown. But building ships takes time. So does expanding shipyard capacity, working through maintenance backlogs and growing the number of qualified Sailors. Even if the Navy makes all the right decisions today, meaningful relief is years away. That leaves an immediate question: What can the Navy do right now to make this new deployment reality more manageable? Retired Admiral Bill Moran , who served as Chief of Naval Personnel and later Vice Chief of Naval Operations, used to emphasize three principles when discussing how the Navy should manage its people: Trust, Balance and Stability. It’s a pretty good way to think about what needs to happen next. Trust begins with being straight with people, especially when the news isn’t good. If a deployment is likely to last ten or eleven months, say so. Don’t build expectations around seven months when everyone knows there’s a good chance the ship will be extended. And when plans change, explain why as soon as operational security allows. Families make real decisions based on deployment schedules. Childcare, jobs, finances, school calendars and family obligations all depend on knowing when someone will be home. Repeated extensions make an already difficult situation considerably worse. Of course, the Navy can’t predict every crisis or operational requirement. Nobody expects it to. But there’s a difference between uncertainty that comes with military operations and uncertainty created by poor communication. Trust also means listening. Navy families know where support systems work and where they don’t. Commanding officers and senior enlisted leaders should have the flexibility to address those problems without turning every reasonable request into a bureaucratic exercise. Nobody joins the Navy expecting an easy life. Long deployments, missed birthdays, holidays and anniversaries come with the profession. Sailors understand that, and their families generally do too. But accepting sacrifice doesn’t mean the Navy gets a pass on making life harder than it needs to be. If ten and eleven month deployments become routine, the Navy should be looking at everything within its authority to offset the additional burden. At sea, that means protecting port visits when possible, improving communications home, ensuring crews get decent food and mail, and finding opportunities for rest. These things may seem small compared with the operational mission, but anyone who’s spent time deployed knows how much they matter. At home, it means making existing family support programs work better. Childcare, emergency assistance and spouse employment support shouldn’t require families to navigate a maze of offices and paperwork. The Navy has programs and resources available. The question is whether they’re easy to access and responsive when people need them. And when ships return, commanders should have the flexibility to ease off requirements that can wait. Not every inspection, training event or administrative task needs to happen immediately after a crew has spent nearly a year at sea. Readiness matters. So does recognizing when people need a break. This may be the toughest part. Operational schedules change. Ships break. Crises happen. Combatant commanders need forces. No one is suggesting the Navy can eliminate those realities. But families need some ability to plan their lives. When deployment schedules, transfers and post-deployment requirements are constantly shifting, even routine decisions become difficult. The Navy should be looking for more flexibility in permanent change of station timing, better coordination between operational and personnel commands, and greater protection for post-deployment recovery periods. That last point deserves particular attention. A Sailor coming home after eleven months at sea doesn’t simply pick up where things left off. Children have grown and changed. Spouses have spent nearly a year handling everything themselves. Families need time to get back into a routine. Giving them that time isn’t a favor. It’s part of keeping Sailors and families healthy enough to continue serving. There’s sometimes a tendency in the military to treat discussions about quality of life as if they’re somehow at odds with warfighting toughness. They aren’t. The Navy needs tough Sailors. It needs people who can endure hardship, operate under pressure and accomplish difficult missions. That’s never going to change. But it also needs leaders who recognize the toll those missions take. A commanding officer who makes communications home a priority isn’t weakening a crew. A senior enlisted leader who helps resolve a family problem isn’t lowering standards. And a fleet commander who protects recovery time after a long deployment isn’t compromising readiness. That’s simply good leadership. There’s also a very practical reason to get this right. The Navy cannot afford to lose experienced Sailors because their families decide that another deployment, another extension or another disrupted year is simply too much. Replacing those Sailors takes time and money. More importantly, the experience they take with them cannot be quickly replaced. The Navy needs more ships, more repair capacity and a stronger maritime industrial base. Admiral Caudle is right to keep pushing those priorities, and Congress and the administration need to help deliver them. But the Sailors deploying today can’t wait for the fleet of the 2030s. There are encouraging signs from Navy leadership. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao has demonstrated a willingness to engage directly with Sailors and put people at the center of his leadership approach. That example matters, particularly when the demands on the force are growing. Combined with the candor shown by Admiral Caudle and MCPON John Perryman, there’s an opportunity to make real progress. The challenge is ensuring that attention at the top translates into meaningful changes throughout the Fleet. Moran’s Trust, Balance and Stability framework provides a useful test. Are we being straight with Sailors and families? Are we doing what we can to ease the burden? Are we giving people enough predictability to manage their lives? These aren’t complicated questions. But answering them honestly, and acting on the answers, takes leadership. The Navy can’t control every operational demand, and it certainly can’t produce new ships overnight. But it has considerable control over how it manages the people it already has. If longer deployments are going to be the norm, then the Navy needs to adjust how it supports the Sailors and families being asked to live with them. We need tough warfighters and resilient families. We also need compassionate leaders who understand that taking care of people is part of maintaining a combat-ready Navy. The Navy can’t build its way out of this problem overnight. But it can lead its way through it, starting now. Chris Servello is co-founder of Provision Advisors and co-host of the CavasShips podcast . articles.title: Venezuelan Oil Exports Remain Stable Despite Stagnant Production, High Freight Rates
articles.summary: Venezuela's oil exports were little changed at 1.08 million barrels per day in October as stagnant crude production and high freight rates continued to curb demand for many South American grades, according to shipping data seen by Reuters on…
articles.body: Venezuelan Oil Exports Remain Stable Despite Stagnant Production, High Freight Rates Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 © Adobe Stock/hamara Venezuela's oil exports were little changed at 1.08 million barrels per day in October as stagnant crude production and high freight rates continued to curb demand for many South American grades, according to shipping data seen by Reuters on Tuesday. The country's oil output and exports have rebounded this year to near pre-sanctions levels following the US capture of then-President Nicolas Maduro in January and a flagship agreement with global traders overseen by Washington. However, growth has recently plateaued as Venezuela's oil and gas producers prepare investments to expand production capacity through imports of drilling rigs and equipment and repairs to state-run PDVSA's ageing infrastructure. A total of 67 vessels departed Venezuelan waters in October carrying crude, fuel, oil products and petrochemicals. Export volumes were down 0.5% from September and the lowest since February, but were 21% higher than a year earlier, the data showed. Exports to the US, the largest destination for Venezuelan crude, fell nearly 29% from the previous month to about 449,000 bpd. Shipments to Europe rose to 235,000 bpd from 86,000 bpd in September. Exports to India edged down to 242,000 bpd from 253,000 bpd, while shipments to Caribbean storage hubs increased to 83,000 bpd from 76,000 bpd. Chevron's exports of Venezuelan crude rose to about 303,000 bpd, their second highest monthly average this year. Shipments handled by traders including Vitol and Trafigura fell to about 506,000 bpd from 637,000 bpd in September, according to the data, which combines PDVSA exports records and vessel-tracking information. (Reuters)

articles.body: Oil Services Industry Face Cost Pressures Amidst Iran Crisis Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Photocreo Bednarek The Iran conflict is causing the oil services industry to increase its cost assessment for projects due to rising shipment, fuel and security costs, which are affecting its Middle Eastern contract performance, executives said at a conference in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. The Iran war, now in its ninth month, has damaged infrastructure and forced staff to evacuate in several countries. Threats to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz have made equipment deliveries difficult, increasing the cost of both labour and insurance. “What we are facing now with our contracts in the Middle East is that logistics costs have increased - sometimes threefold. Fuel costs have doubled, labour costs have increased 30 to 40 percent,” said Alessandro Bernini, chief executive of Italian engineering group Maire. The cost jump is eating into margins of service companies, raising the cost of projects and ultimately translating into higher energy prices and inflation around the world, he said. Logistics have become a problem due to the difficulty of delivering equipment, said Alessandro Puliti, CEO of Italian energy contractor Saipem. “We have been sitting outside Hormuz for months,” he told the conference. Oil services company NESR, which has operations in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Oman and Iraq, said the biggest increase in costs was in shipping and logistics, as it had to store materials in warehouses for much longer to cover for possible disruptions. Companies are absorbing those cost increases, its CEO said. “You eat it most of the time. You are not happy but you just move on. C’est la vie,” said NESR chief executive Sherif Foda. (Reuters)

articles.title: Hormuz Standoff Leaves Both Sides With Economic Pain
articles.summary: As US President Donald Trump threatens renewed attacks against Iran, Tehran’s intermittent strikes on commercial vessels have left the two sides locked in a painful economic standoff.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz are visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, August 28, 2026. Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS By Gerry Doyle (Bloomberg) — As US President Donald Trump threatens renewed attacks against Iran, Tehran’s intermittent strikes on commercial vessels have left the two sides locked in a painful economic standoff. For Iran, the US blockade of its oil exports has snuffed out a key part of its military funding and severely hobbled the $300 billion economy, with only a tiny fraction of the prewar 2 million barrels per day are leaving the country via land routes. And for the US, the rising cost of shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz — even though US Central Command says almost all Iranian attacks there fail or are intercepted — has kept fuel prices high, stirring a political backlash at home with the midterm elections fast approaching. Iran doesn’t even need a high tempo of attacks to keep oil prices elevated; although shipments through the strait are at about 80% of prewar levels, the associated risk has inflated insurance costs. It was more expensive in early October to hire a supertanker in some parts of the world than it was to send a rocket into space. But even significant economic pain isn’t likely to change Iran’s ability to keep up “harassing fire” in the strait, said Jim Lamson, a visiting research fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London and former CIA analyst focused on Iran and the Middle East. A stockpile of missile components means Tehran can continue to assemble anti-ship weapons, even though US airstrikes have severely degraded its ability to manufacture them at scale, he said. “They have been planning for a long-term asymmetric conflict with the US for decades,” Lamson said. “Things like building in resilience, building in redundancy, building in stockpiling — these have been part of their military culture.” Although there were a record of at least 28 open-source reports of damage to shipping in the strait in October, Iran has not increased its volume of attacks, according to a US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Instead, more serious damage has led to more incidents being flagged, with a quarter of the reports in the first two weeks of October involving strikes on ships’ engine rooms, which can take vessels out of service. US forces reportedly struck Iranian positions on Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz overnight. Trump, meanwhile, has expressed hope for negotiations. The continued attacks by Iran leave a few options — none of them with a guaranteed favorable outcome. Trump may order the resumption of airstrikes after the election, even though these only go so far to completely shut down Iran’s ability to lob missiles into the strait — typically unsophisticated weapons that attack any ship in a target area. That leaves making the economic cost of Iranian ship attacks impossible to bear, said John Miller, a retired US Navy vice admiral and former head of the Navy element of CENTCOM. “As long as they want to have a blockade in place, they can continue to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz,” Miller said of Iran. “This has always been the case: You can either make them unwilling or unable.” The tanker industry is continuing to send oil out of the Middle East for now at near prewar levels, and it’s not clear what sort of escalation it would take to halt that. Transits through the waterway are earning owners of supertankers tens of millions of dollars, and the vessels’ crews several months’ pay for a few days of dangerous navigation. For now that’s proving sufficient to keep trade running. The International Maritime Organization estimates that there have been 121 incidents in Hormuz and the wider region since the war began, including 24 confirmed seafarer fatalities. No ship has struck a floating mine while transiting the strait, the US official said, although Iran said as recently as late October that a mine damaged a tanker, and on Friday the UKMTO, which monitors shipping security, reported a tanker was damaged by explosives placed on its hull. Iran is using both traditional cruise missiles and drones to attack shipping, the official said, and US forces are both organizing ship transits and protecting them, largely with aircraft overhead. CENTCOM has said about 95% of ships transit the strait without incident. The US works directly with the shipping industry, sharing information and discussing timing, routes and numbers for vessels that want to pass through the strait in either direction, the US official said. US forces then formulate a plan for doing so safely, including what assets will be used to keep tabs on the journey and shoot down threats if necessary. Miller said much of Iran’s ability to track anything beyond visual range of its shores had been all but destroyed over the last eight months. As a result, the weapons it uses are often fired blind, or at the general area where Iranian strike planners think ships might be. Once the missiles arrive, radar or infrared seekers guide them to whatever is nearby. Aircraft armed with cheap munitions such as the APKWS missile, which costs about $20,000 for a BAE Systems Plc guidance kit, handle those sorts of attacks. The expensive and advanced air-defense interceptors on US Navy ships, such as the Raytheon SM-6 and SM-3 Block IIA, are then reserved for ballistic missile threats. Trump has previewed in recent days plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. But it’s not clear that airstrikes — especially against an adversary that has planned for decades to keep key capabilities safe against such attacks — will change the situation in the strait, said Emma Salisbury, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute and an associate fellow at the Royal Navy Strategic Studies Centre. A surge in fighting could push oil prices into the $120-$130 range, according to analysis by Bloomberg Economics chief emerging markets economist Ziad Daoud.
